commits.pr_title: [ROCm] Update ROCm to 10.1 and MORI to v1.2.4 and amd-smi fixes
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

This PR updates the current ROCm `Dockerfile.rocm_base` to `10.1` and `MORI `to `v1.2.4`.

Things to note:

  * Cherry-picks over changes from https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62531
  * `rocm-smi_lib` was removed from `10.1`
  * It's no longer necessary to `pip install amd-smi` anymore, its included in `10.1`
  * `MORI` version `v1.2.3.post1` doesn't have https://github.com/ROCm/mori/pull/663 but `v1.2.4` does, which builds with `10.1`
  *  The ROCR  fixes needed in `10.0` needed to be updated for `10.1` (applying the patch to the newer version in rocm-systems) [users/rasmith/10.1/hsa_gpu_edge_signal](https://github.com/ROCm/rocm-systems/compare/develop...users/rasmith/10.1/hsa_gpu_edge_signal)
  * `amd-smi` is the replacement for `rocm-smi`, but this broke a number of things:
    *  kv connector tests
    * any test that was using `rocm-smi` before
  * Fixed any breakage caused by the `rocm-smi` removal and made it use `amd-smi`
  * Needed to add a Python `.pth` file so `amd-smi` can always be found, without having to change the Dockerfile or always have to ensure one doesn't forget to add it to `PYTHONPATH`.  We might need to file an issue so that it gets installed properly through the usual Rock wheel installs.
  * `Ray` needed to be updated since the current version depends on `rocm-smi`, but the newer versions now use `amd-smi`.
  * Update the ROCm kernel symbol map tool to recognize the device code that ROCm 10.1's compiler produces, so kernel-based CI test selection keeps working, see https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59100.
  * Need AITER `v0.1.28.post1` for to avoid the perf loss due to 10.1 compiler change

### Extra

`amd-smi` has an option if you want the old `rocm-smi` output:
   * `amd-smi --rocm-smi`
## Claims

* Dockerfile builds
* Preserves ROCR performance benefits
* CI parity (TDB)
* Image and wheel pipeline still works (TBD)

## Validation

* Dockerfile needs to build
* Will need parity with CI
* Did a run with the ROCR fixes to check performance still preserved.

## Details

### ROCR performance check

Performance run to check that the ROCR performance fixes are preserved:

 | model | tp | num-prompts | on tok/s | off tok/s | delta | TPOT on/off (ms) | TTFT on/off (ms) |
 |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
 | Llama-3.1-8B | 4 | 10 | 475.79 | 394.30 | +20.7% | 2.08 / 2.52 | 21.52 / 21.53 |
 | gpt-oss-120b | 8 | 30 | 187.53 | 139.40 | +34.5% | 5.31 / 7.15 | 26.82 / 28.26 |
 | GLM-5.2-FP8 (AITER=1) | 8 | 10 | 80.42 | 66.24 | +21.4% | 12.31 / 14.97 | 139.59 / 140.38 |

Currently builds:

Result of:

`DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 docker build -f docker/Dockerfile.rocm_base --build-arg -t vllm-base:rocm10_1 .`

was

```
=> [final 6/6] RUN echo "BASE_IMAGE: ubuntu:22.04" > /app/versions.txt     && echo "PYTHON_VERSION: 3.12" >> /app/versions.txt     && echo "ROCM_SDK_VERSION: 10.1.0" >> /app/versions.txt     && echo "T  2.4s
 => exporting to image                                                                                                                                                                                      6.1s
 => => exporting layers                                                                                                                                                                                     6.1s
 => => writing image sha256:640f8b0d8f1ea2c03f5ec637a9b0bb13cbd2d729c43863ec26be7b82734784d5                                                                                                                0.0s
 => => naming to docker.io/library/vllm-base:rocm10_1                                
```   

Commands used to benchmark were:

 ```
vllm serve "$MODEL" --dtype auto -tp "$TP" --port 8620 \
    --no-enable-prefix-caching --disable-uvicorn-access-log --trust-remote-code \
    --max-model-len 101372 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 &

  vllm bench serve --model "$MODEL" --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8620 \
    --trust-remote-code --percentile-metrics tpot,ttft,itl,e2el \
    --dataset-name random --ignore-eos --temperature 0 \
    --max-concurrency 1 --num-prompts "$NP" \
    --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 1024 \
    --ready-check-timeout-sec 1800 \
    --save-result --result-filename bench.json
```

---

### Import and Install Ability

Since `amdsmi` is now included in 10.1 but is not a complete package,  I needed to add an `amdsmi` build step in the Dockerfile and make sure that the vLLM wheels would still work when users install them.  I wanted to detail the results of that here.

Every table below compares the same five vLLM builds. Tables that only concern this PR use the three 10.1 ones.

- **7.2.3** — vLLM v0.32.0, shipped.
- **10.0** — vLLM nightly, shipped.
- **10.1 base** (`bd84cb1a6f`) — this PR before the `.pth` was added. amdsmi via `ENV PYTHONPATH`.
- **10.1 .pth** (`513d206965`) — what the PR has carried since. amdsmi via a `.pth`.
- **10.1 PR** (`bc5e7f00d6`) — this change. amdsmi installed as a package.

The three 10.1 columns were measured on images built from those commits.

Every measurement is on one host with **8 GPUs** (gfx950 / MI355X), so a correct amdsmi reports 8. A 0 means it enumerated none.

#### How amdsmi reaches the user

| | 7.2.3 | 10.0 | 10.1 base | 10.1 .pth | 10.1 PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| In the image | Installed wheel | Installed, plus `ENV PYTHONPATH` | `ENV PYTHONPATH` | `.pth` file | Installed wheel |
| vLLM wheel pins amdsmi | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ |
| Loader patch | Not needed | `find_spec` lookup | None | None | `.patch` file |

#### In the Docker image

| | 7.2.3 | 10.0 | 10.1 base | 10.1 .pth | 10.1 PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `import amdsmi` when CI sets PYTHONPATH | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Run a model when CI sets PYTHONPATH | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ |
| `pip show amdsmi` | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |

**This is why the `.pth` was added.** CI's `run-amd-test.sh` sets `PYTHONPATH=/vllm-workspace`, replacing the `ENV PYTHONPATH` the base image relied on. `import amdsmi` then raises `ModuleNotFoundError`, vLLM falls back to `UnspecifiedPlatform`, and running a model fails with `RuntimeError: Device string must not be empty`. A `.pth` lives in site-packages, so nothing a caller puts in `PYTHONPATH` can displace it. An installed package has the same property. Without that override every column works, so the override is the whole of the difference.

#### Installing the vLLM wheel on a clean machine

A stock `python:3.12` container — no ROCm, no vLLM — with the GPUs passed through, following the install docs:

```bash
uv venv --python 3.12 --seed --managed-python
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install <that commit's vLLM wheel>
```

The vLLM wheel contains no amdsmi files and ships no `.pth`. It only declares `Requires-Dist: amdsmi==...`, and the index serves amdsmi as a separate 87 KB wheel that pip pulls in — the same arrangement as torch and triton.

Nothing from the ROCm image exists here, so each column is only what its own wheel brings:

| | base (pins unpatched) | .pth (pins nothing) | PR (pins patched) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pip show amdsmi` | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ |
| `import amdsmi` on its own | ❌ `OSError` | ❌ `ModuleNotFoundError` | ✅ |
| `import torch`, then `import amdsmi` | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ |
| vLLM detects the GPUs | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ |
| Run a model | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ |

**`.pth` is the regression:** no pin, so no amdsmi, so `UnspecifiedPlatform` and `RuntimeError: Device string must not be empty`.

Two independent problems sit behind those red cells:

- **No pin.** The build pins whatever is *installed*, and a `.pth` installs nothing — so amdsmi quietly dropped out of the vLLM wheel's requirements. It was not removed on purpose.
- **An unpatched loader.** base does install amdsmi, but its copy cannot find the AMD SMI library unless something has already loaded it. vLLM survives this because it imports torch first. A bare `import amdsmi` does not.

The PR fixes both: an amdsmi wheel built from the SDK's own sources with the loader patched, installed in the image and pinned by the vLLM wheel.

#### Installing the vLLM wheel: inside the image, three ways

The same wheels, but installed **inside that commit's own vLLM image** rather than on a clean machine, with the image's own vLLM uninstalled first. The contrast with the table above is the point: here the image's `.pth` or `ENV PYTHONPATH` still exists and can rescue an install that the wheel alone would not. Three ways to make the environment — the image's system Python, a plain `python3 -m venv`, and the documented `uv venv --managed-python`.

| after installing that commit's wheel | base | .pth | PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| system `python3`: `import amdsmi` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| system `python3`: `pip show amdsmi` | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ |
| `python3 -m venv`: `import amdsmi` | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ |
| `uv venv --managed-python`: `import amdsmi` | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ |
| GPUs reported in a venv, after `import torch` (8 is correct) | **0** | no amdsmi to ask | **8** |
| which amdsmi a venv ends up using | the image's SDK copy, via `PYTHONPATH` | none | the venv's own |

**A `.pth` is the one mechanism a user's own virtual environment throws away.** It lives in the image's site-packages, so neither venv recipe sees it, and that state has no pin to install amdsmi instead.

**`ENV PYTHONPATH` surviving a venv is a liability, not a feature.** Base's pin does install amdsmi into the venv, but `PYTHONPATH` then shadows it with the image's SDK copy, which pairs with the venv's own torch and reports **0 GPUs** instead of 8 — a wrong answer rather than an error.

#### Building vLLM from source

Two kinds of editable install are tested:

```bash
python3 setup.py develop   # what the ROCm install docs prescribe. `pip install .` does not work there
pip install -e .
```

Both run inside that commit's own image against a bind-mounted checkout, with `PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH=gfx950`, after removing the vLLM the image ships so it cannot shadow the build. They agree on every row below.

| after either editable install | base | .pth | PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| The build succeeds | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| `pip show amdsmi` | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |
| `import amdsmi` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Run a model | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Run a model when CI sets PYTHONPATH | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ |

The last row is the developer-facing form of the CI failure: build editable on base under that `PYTHONPATH` and vLLM cannot run a model.

The docs' amdsmi step, which a source builder outside these images still needs:

| | 7.2.3 | 10.0 | 10.1 base | 10.1 .pth | 10.1 PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| The documented step runs clean | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |
| Lines in that step | 1 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 4 |
| `pip show amdsmi` afterwards | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |

The 10.1 SDK stopped shipping packaging metadata, so the documented `pip install` fails there. The PR's step supplies that metadata and the loader patch itself, and shrinks back to one line once a future SDK restores it.

## Motivation

Mooncake provides an expert-parallel all-to-all communication backend for MoE models. This PR proposes integrating Mooncake EP into vLLM as an optional `mooncake_ep` A2A backend.

Mooncake EP has already been integrated into SGLang. We would like to bring the backend to vLLM and discuss the appropriate evolution path with the vLLM community.

## Changes

- Add `mooncake_ep` to the A2A backend registry.
- Add the Mooncake EP CUDA communicator manager.
- Add `MooncakeEPPrepareAndFinalize`.
- Integrate Mooncake EP with the modular `FusedMoEKernel` path.
- Add a two-GPU kernel/adapter correctness test covering:
  - Mooncake dispatch and combine;
  - reference local-expert execution;
  - modular `FusedMoEKernel` execution;
  - BF16 inputs with different token counts.

The implementation follows the existing vLLM EP integration patterns used by DeepEP, NIXL-EP, and MoonEP. The Mooncake dependency remains optional and is detected through vLLM's package probe mechanism.

## Testing

Tested on two H20 GPUs with:

- PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130
- Mooncake 0.3.13.post1

```bash
pytest -q tests/kernels/moe/test_mooncake_ep.py
```

```text
6 passed
```

We would be happy to work with the vLLM community on the evolution of this integration. Please let me know if there is any additional information, testing, or implementation change that would help with the review.

commits.pr_body:
## Why?

Fixes [#69660](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/69660)

Inkling 2 fails during startup with Triton 3.9 because its attention kernel calls the removed `_reinterpret` method.

Reason: [triton-lang/triton#11131](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/pull/11131) renamed the descriptor method to `reinterpret`.
Predecessor: [vllm-project/vllm#60324](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/60324), which upgrades Triton to 3.9.0.
The version gate also preserves support for older Triton versions, so this fix can merge before the predecessor.

## Overview

Select the `_verify_p` implementation at import time, with the version gate pattern from `vllm/model_executor/layers/mamba/ops/mamba_ssm.py`.
Use `reinterpret` for Triton >= 3.9.0 and `_reinterpret` for older versions.

## Claims

- Address the confirmed Inkling-2-Mini startup failure with `vllm/vllm-openai:cu135-nightly`.
- Preserve the older descriptor API for Triton < 3.9.0.
- Preserve the descriptor dtype, shape, layout, and subsequent tensor operations.

## Validation

The reporter reproduced the missing-method error with a standalone Gluon kernel.
The reporter then confirmed successful model startup after the same replacement inside the container.
The failing container used vLLM `0.34.0rc1.dev1235+gf2f9edcac.d20261124.cu135`, PyTorch `2.16.0.dev20261116+cu135`, and Triton `3.9.0+gitb7ddcf86`.

Reproduction command:

```bash
docker run --gpus all \
  --privileged --ipc=host -p 8000:8000 \
  vllm/vllm-openai:cu135-nightly \
  thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini \
  --tensor-parallel-size 1 \
  --max-model-len 262144 \
  --reasoning-parser inkling \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}'
```

Before the replacement:

```text
p = s_tmem._reinterpret(gl.bfloat16, [2, BLOCK_M, 2 * BLOCK_N], layout)
    ^
AttributeError("'tensor_memory_descriptor' object has no attribute '_reinterpret'")
```

Local checks passed on commit `798ff2251c006a9dd1d542b5a96a57df153a71e1` with Python 3.14.6 and Ruff 0.17.2:

```bash

.venv/bin/python -m py_compile vllm/models/inkling2/nvidia/ops/attention.py
git diff HEAD^ HEAD --check
```

```text
All checks passed!
1 file already formatted
```

CUDA tests and model accuracy evaluation did not run locally; the preparation host is a Mac without a CUDA GPU.
Full pre-commit checks did not run.
The existing B200 Inkling suite includes `tests/models/inkling2/test_attention.py::test_inkling2_rel_decode_attention`, which covers verification against a reference.

The reporter confirmation covers the original method replacement. CUDA validation of the version gate remains pending.
Run the existing test with both Triton 3.8 and 3.9:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/models/inkling2/test_attention.py::test_inkling2_rel_decode_attention -v
```

## Details

Duplicate searches found no open PR for this descriptor rename. PR #60324 updates dependencies; this PR updates the affected kernel call.
Unrelated helpers with `_reinterpret` in their names retain their current names.
The change restores existing model support and adds no configuration or new feature.

commits.pr_title: [Kernel][Perf] Do not split rows no longer than k in `top_k_per_row_decode`
commits.pr_body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

When the logits are at least 200,000 wide, `top_k_per_row_decode` spends about 120 µs on a decode row shorter than k, and about 60 µs on a row of exactly k, although the result is just the row's own indices. In a small batch, a row of 2–4K tokens takes about 50 µs. The call ends with its slowest row, so one such short row slows the whole batch. This PR lets rows no longer than k skip the split and the merge, which brings them to about 5 µs.

This matters for Mistral Large 4 on MI325X, which uses this kernel at its default 262,144 context with k = 2048.

## Claims

- Calls on rows no longer than k drop from 43–142 µs to 5–10 µs on MI325X, at k ∈ {512, 1024, 2048} and widths of 262,144 and 1,048,576. On MI355X, rows of exactly k get 2.2–2.7× faster at k = 1024, through gfx950's own split launch, and 3.25–3.45× faster at k = 2048.
- Batches that mix such rows with longer ones get faster too, by up to 2.5× at k = 2048, because the call no longer waits on the short rows.
- Mistral Large 4 (TP8, 8× MI325X, 262,144 context) with 1K-token inputs: median time per output token −15% to −27% (19.21 → 14.08 ms at concurrency 1), output throughput +17% to +36%. With 8K-token inputs, where no row is that short, results match main within 0.5%.
- Longer rows pay for one extra length load in the merge: a median of +0.5 µs on MI325X and +0.35 µs on MI355X. No configuration is more than 3% slower than main on either AMD GPU, and GSM8K accuracy is unchanged.
- On an H200 (CUDA), rows of exactly k get 3.1–3.8× faster. Longer rows change by −0.6 to +2.0 µs (at most +4%), of which 0.32–0.58 µs is the merge's extra length load. The raw output is in the review thread.
- The output contract is unchanged, and the decision is made on the device, so captured graphs stay valid as lengths change.

## Validation

### Unit tests

`test_top_k_per_row_decode_split_work_short_rows` replays one captured graph at k ∈ {512, 1024, 2048}, width 262,144 and next_n = 2, while the device-side lengths move rows across k (lengths 0, 1, k − 1, k, k + 1, 3k, width − 1 and width). It checks exact top-k against `torch.topk` and that each row is its valid indices followed by `-1`. With 8 rows, k = 1024 also reaches gfx950's own split launch, which this PR changes too. Main's kernel passes it as well: its result is correct, only slow.

```
================ 3 passed, 979 deselected, 17 warnings in 2.33s ================
```

The skips need CUDA or gfx950; the file runs in full in :amd: (MI300) Core Operation Kernels, :nvidia: (H100) DeepSeek V4 Kernels and :nvidia: (B200) Kernels. On an H200, the new test passes on main's kernel and on this PR's too.

Each indexer layer selects k = 2048, so every decode row is no longer than k until the sequence passes 2,048 tokens. ## Details

**Root cause.** From 200,000 columns (`kSplitWorkThreshold`), every row is split into 10 blocks whose 10·k candidates are then merged. When a row has no more than k logits, each block gets fewer than k and pads its candidates with -FLT_MAX. If the row is shorter than k, the k-th largest candidate is one of those padding values. The merge is a radix select, and on each of its passes it refines the bin that holds the k-th value, so the at least 9·k identical padding candidates all fall into it and their shared-memory atomics serialize. A row of exactly k does not serialize, but still pays for the split and the merge.

**Change.** In the split kernel, a row no longer than k now runs only in its first block, which takes the existing `rowLen <= topK` shortcut and writes the row's indices, then `-1` padding, straight to the output. The row's other blocks exit at once and the merge skips the row. The split and the merge both decide from the row's device-side length, so nothing is read back to the host and a captured graph stays valid as lengths change. The diff is +21/−8 lines in `top_k_per_row.cu` and adds no instantiation or shared memory. The output contract is unchanged: `min(row_end, k)` indices, then `-1`.

**Who hits it.** Decode logits are `max_model_len` wide under full graphs, so this path runs for models served with a context of at least 200,000 tokens, however long the requests actually are. Mistral Large 4 at its default 262,144 is one, and on gfx942 this kernel is its only decode top-k: AITER's decode top-k is used only on gfx950. DeepSeek V3.2 (`max_model_len` 163,840) stays below the threshold. On such a server, a decode step is slow whenever at least one request in the batch has at most k = 2,048 tokens so far. Every request with a shorter prompt spends its first decode steps there and slows down the requests batched with it. Examples are short chat turns, routing and classification calls, and few-shot evals such as 5-shot GSM8K. Traffic in which every prompt is longer than k, such as agents with long system prompts, never takes the new path and only pays the 0.5 µs below.

**Tradeoffs.**

- Rows longer than k are split and merged as before, but the merge now loads the row's length, which costs them a median of 0.5 µs on MI325X and 0.35 µs on MI355X, and at most 3%. On H200 the same load costs the merge 0.32–0.58 µs, and a call at most 4%.
- Running longer rows in one block too would help homogeneous batches: one block beats the 10-block split up to about 16K logits. But in a batch that mixes rows on both sides of such a cutoff, the long single-block rows hold up the merge of the split rows. With a 16K cutoff that batch got up to 70% slower than main with clustered logits, so this PR stops at k. A follow-up can instead pick the number of blocks from the row length rather than the buffer width, as gfx950's top-512 path does (gfx950TopK512ActiveBlocks), if it keeps such mixed batches from getting slower. The review thread has the numbers for k < L ≤ 10·k on H200 and MI325X. gfx950's three-block k = 1024 launch for more than 64 rows (`topKPerRowDecodeDeviceLengthAware`) pads rows of at most k in the same way and is left to that follow-up too.
- The change applies on every platform and to both split launches (the generic one and gfx950's k = 1024 one), since it only removes work. The serving runs and the kernel sweep were on MI325X, and the tests and the in-tree benchmark also ran on MI355X and on an H200. On CUDA, the indexer's `auto` top-k backend picks `cooperative_topk` or `persistent_topk` for k ∈ {512, 1024, 2048} (`_resolve_auto` in `vllm/model_executor/layers/indexer_topk.py`), so this path runs there only for other k or when `per_row` is requested.

**Not a duplicate.** I searched open PRs for `top_k_per_row_decode`, `topKPerRowDecode` and `kSplitWorkThreshold`. The closest is #67367, which keeps 16–36K rows in one block on gfx950's separate top-512 path. This PR changes the generic split, which is what Mistral Large 4 uses on gfx942. #57844 and #50470 change how ROCm routes decode top-k, not this kernel.
